records.name: Trinidad and Tobago
records.summary:
Trinidad and Tobago demands real caution from trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the colonial buggery laws (Jones v. AG, 2018, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still “beaten, stoned and chopped,” with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of Grindr ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including a Cocorite man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.

sources.claim: Trinidad and Tobago Newsday (July 2024): 'Long way yet for recognition, safe spaces' - TT Transgender Coalition director Rae Alibey says the trans community is the most marginalised and not even recognised in T&T; gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation; gender-identity markers on institutional forms are absent; national discussions and attitudinal research needed.

Newsday (Nov 2024): police warning over cyber criminals - Grindr hook-ups ending in cars, cash and phones stolen; criminals create fake dating accounts to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings followed by armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault; two separate incidents reported in one week.

Newsday editorial (June 2024): 'Grind hate to a halt' - a spate of Grindr-related attacks (almost half a dozen in recent months); Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne points to gaps in the law: 'We don't have a specific hate crime category in legislation'; the editorial argues the gap must be closed.

CNC3 (Aug 2024): CAISO head unhappy LGBTQ rights reform ignored again - the PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected reform of sexual-orientation rights; CAISO had recommended adding sexual orientation and gender identity to protected statuses under section 4 of the Constitution; 'no political party has stepped up'.

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Trinidad & Tobago' (Aug 2012): although homosexuality is illegal, 'the laws are mostly ignored' - context of the islands' history from Spanish colonisation through British rule.

PinkNews (Nov 2017) by Jason Jones: 'I am a criminal simply because I am a gay man' - his High Court challenge to Trinidad and Tobago's laws (up to 25 years for 'serious indecency'); ~100,000 LGBT people live under the threat; the laws were inherited from Britain but extended to lesbians after independence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (June 2016): PM Keith Rowley claimed the state must protect all citizens 'regardless of whom they sleep with', but said there were no plans to amend the buggery laws and declined to address the EOC's call for anti-discrimination protection.

records.name: Tunisia
records.summary:
Tunisia is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — the country is in an active crackdown. Between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025, authorities arrested at least 84 people in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity — mostly gay men and transgender women, per Amnesty International. Penal Code Articles 226 bis (public indecency) and 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) are applied to effectively criminalise gender expression, and enforcement disproportionately targets transgender women.

In detention, trans women are processed under birth names and housed in men's prisons, where local NGO Intersection documents severe abuse. The courts have hardened: in April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused legal gender recognition to a trans man, dismissing gender dysphoria as “mental illness.” Since President Saied's 2021 power consolidation, the post-revolution space for LGBT organising (Shams, Damj) has been crushed — Shams was dissolved.

sources.claim: Amnesty International (Feb 2025): Tunisia steps up crackdown on LGBTI individuals with a wave of arrests - at least 84 people (mainly gay men and trans women) arrested, arbitrarily detained and unjustly prosecuted between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025 in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef, solely based on actual or perceived SOGI, per Damj Association.

Cairo 52 country review of Tunisia: gender identities/expressions deviating from norms are effectively criminalised via Penal Code Articles 226 bis and 230, disproportionately targeting trans women; no comprehensive legal gender recognition framework - inconsistent rulings relying on judges' personal views and Sharia interpretations; gender-affirming care accessible only through well-informed medical professionals.

Intersection Association (Nov 2024): transgender women in Tunisian prisons endure continuous suffering - processed under former names and gender identification in all official procedures; forced shaving on entry without consent causes profound psychological harm, targeting the essence of their gender identity.

Cairo 52 (Jan 2024): the Tunis Court of First Instance (April 2023) declined legal gender recognition to a trans man, asserting insufficient evidence of a biological medical condition and dismissing gender identity disorder as a mental illness not fulfilling LGR criteria - reasoning based on comparative law from Egypt, ECtHR case-law and Dar Al-Ifta religious opinions.
HRW (March 2016): 'Tunisia: Men Prosecuted for Homosexuality' - documents prosecutions under Article 230 and the use of forced anal examinations as 'evidence'.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Sept 2017): Tunisia pledged to the UN to stop forced anal testing (minister Mehdi Ben Gharbia in Geneva) but did not accept repeal of Article 230 (up to 3 years); Shams president Mounir Baatour was unenthusiastic - the abusive 'test' was dropped but the law remains.

records.name: Turkey
records.summary:
Turkey presents real, structured danger for trans visitors — institutionalised, presidential-level hostility that has become state policy. Police profile and detain trans women for identity checks (20 were detained in Istanbul in July 2025), trans women have historically been "frequent targets of torture and ill-treatment" by police, and a trans woman attacked with a knife was herself detained (victim-criminalised). A draft law leaked in October 2025 would criminalise LGBT people — not yet passed but under active government consideration.

Transphobic attacks and Pride-event violence are documented, the Health Ministry is introducing regulations that may profile and restrict trans healthcare, and foreign visitors must carry original passports at all times — creating outing risk at the frequent transit checkpoints. If detained, trans women are placed in men's facilities with documented rights violations.

The risk is concentrated in urban trans-visible contexts (Istanbul's Beyoğlu/Tarlabaşı) rather than package-holiday tourist zones, but the institutional hostility pervades. Turkey is outside the Schengen area.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Oct 2025): 'Türkiye: Draft Law Threatens LGBT People with Prison' — a proposed penal-code package would effectively criminalise LGBT people with long prison terms.

Kaos GL (Feb 2026): 'A major siege' against LGBTI+ people in 2025 - hostility turned into state policy; the LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 ('The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People') documents institutionalised anti-LGBTI policies, hate speech from senior officials, and instructions to public institutions under the 'Year of the Family' banner creating a climate encouraging human-rights violations.

bianet (Aug 2025): Istanbul police detain ~20 trans women for ID checks amid profiling concerns - stopped on the street, while shopping or in cafés in Beyoğlu, held at Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released after 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks; legal experts argue GBT checks violate ECHR Article 5; one detainee: 'They didn't fine us, but they documented us. The new law hasn't even passed yet, but they're already enforcing it on us.'
Turkish Minute (Feb 2026): report documents sharp rise in LGBTQ rights violations in Turkey in 2025 - coverage of the Kaos GL report findings.

Truth Justice Memory Center et al. (Aug 2025): 'You should have behaved yourself!' - 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week monitoring report by seven human-rights organisations documenting violations during and after the 11th Trans Pride March and 23rd Istanbul LGBTI+ Pride March; systematic violations ongoing since 2015, with senior officials using discriminatory rhetoric.

Kaos GL (Sept 2025): a new Health Ministry regulation may profile trans people and restrict transition access - 'gender reassignment' added to official reasons for medical board reports; e-reports replace paper; boards must now include six specialities examining applicants separately; the ministry says it 'does not grant a new right' but strengthens 'control and monitoring mechanisms'.

Kaos GL (Aug 2024): transphobic attack in Istanbul - trans woman Yaşam was attacked with a knife by a 17-year-old in Bakırköy; the victim was detained and spent the night in a detention centre while the attacker was released; 'The detention of the victim trans woman, not the knife attacker, reveals the hate policy of the Turkish state.'
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (timeout); the underlying Nomad Lawyer piece (2026) covers Turkey's passport-carrying rule, fines and detention warnings.

Human Rights Watch (May 2008): launch of the 123-page report 'We Need a Law for Liberation' — documents a long, continuing history of violence and abuse based on sexual orientation and gender identity and calls for legal reform, urging the EU to tie membership prospects to ending the abuses.

records.name: Tuvalu
records.summary: Tuvalu demands real caution. Male same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced); no LGR; very small, tight-knit, church-centred society; no specifically documented anti-trans violence (population ~11,000). Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.claim: ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Tuvalu: documents the legal status — male same-sex conduct criminalised under colonial-era provisions.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Tuvalu: traditional customs perpetuate religious and social discrimination including against women; no government abuses; the LGBT section notes criminalisation under the Penal Code but no prosecutions.

Tuvalu Ministry of Health Global AIDS Progress Report 2017 (UNAIDS): the national HIV response, drawing on the Pacific Multi-Country Mapping and Behavioural Study on HIV and STI risk vulnerability among key populations (including MSM and transgender Tuvaluans).
US Mission in Geneva (March 2011): post on LGBT rights in the UN context - Tuvalu was among Pacific countries signing the joint statement of support for decriminalisation and SOGI rights.

GlobalGayz archive of Tuvalu news and reports: includes the OHCHR op-ed 'Decriminalizing Homosexuality - first step to establish equality' (Oct 2011) noting Tuvalu among Pacific countries supporting the UN call.

records.name: Taiwan
records.summary:
Taiwan is a progressive Asian destination — it was the first in Asia to legalise same-sex marriage (2019), the government is investing US$8.76 million to double gender-neutral public bathrooms by 2029, and a trans march in Taipei drew 3,000 participants in 2025. There are no documented severe incidents (no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, or organised dating-app predation).

The main gaps are legal-gender-recognition reform stagnation — a 2008 Ministry order still requires sex-reassignment surgery to change one's gender marker (blocking an estimated 90% of trans people, with only case-by-case court exceptions), and the government has been "floundering" on reform — and a rising anti-gender discourse movement that has produced online waves of hostility. A trans woman was outed during a police identity inspection (the Viva case), and Taipei has held a vigil for victims of anti-trans violence.

For a visitor, bathrooms are unrestricted (and being proactively expanded to gender-neutral), there is no criminalisation, and border/immigration poses no trans-specific friction. Taipei City has trans-friendly service guidelines.

sources.claim: Taiwan Insight (Feb 2026): 'What about trans rights? Taiwan's ongoing struggle for self-ID' - the 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery to change legal gender blocks an estimated 90% of trans people from obtaining matching national ID; every ID-requiring aspect of daily life (clinics, airport security) becomes a potential site of distress and discrimination; the Ministry of Health and Welfare has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013.

Taiwan Insight (Jan 2026): the Taiwanese government continues to flounder on transgender rights in 2025 amidst continued transphobia - no tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction; pending conscription-criteria changes could actively harm trans people; anti-gender movement activity rising, with organisations supporting Trump's anti-trans policies and the Taiwan Solidarity Party calling for a 'two genders' position.

Taipei Times (Aug 2024): the Ministry of Environment will invest NT$280 million over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms nationwide (623 to 1,246 by 2029); of trans and gender-neutral survey respondents reporting discrimination, 17% occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms.

Focus Taiwan (Nov 2025): 'Most Taiwan all-gender restrooms do not meet standards: Rights group' — an LGBTQ+ rights group finds only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404 - page removed); the underlying page addressed Taiwan's transgender rights - laws, protections and gaps.
New Bloom (Nov 2024): analysis of the wave of anti-gender discourse in Taiwan - rising anti-gender movement activity and its political context.

TaiwanPlus (Aug 2024): a Taipei court denied a transgender woman's request to change the gender marker on her government ID without requiring surgery or a psychological evaluation; the supporting rights group says they will likely appeal.

JURIST dispatch (Nov 2025): the 7th annual Taiwan Transgender March in Taipei drew an estimated 3,000 people despite rain, with international participants; calls for an end to discrimination against trans people as the rights debate continues.

Utopia Asia Taiwan travel and resources page: 'one of Asia's most progressive countries for LGBT rights, and certainly the most liberal of the Chinese diaspora'; notes Taiwan regularised adoption for same-sex parents on May 16, 2023; listings of organisations, bars, spas and venues across 12 cities.

records.name: Tanzania
records.summary:
Tanzania is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex activity with up to life imprisonment, and the political environment has been actively hostile since the Magufuli-era crackdowns (arrests, forced anal examinations documented by HRW in earlier years, de-registration of LGBT-serving organisations). The 2024 case of Mauzinde is emblematic: a transgender woman and activist found abandoned in a forest in Rahaleo, beaten, her ears cut off — an attack the UN Human Rights Office called “horrendous.”

OONI documented extensive targeted blocking of LGBTQ websites correlating with the escalating crackdown, and Amnesty's 2024 regional report notes Tanzanian pushes to further criminalise LGBT people. Zanzibar has its own, harsher penal code. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest under indecency provisions and mob violence; Zanzibar is worse than the mainland.

sources.claim: JURIST (June 2024): the UN Human Rights Office denounced the 'horrendous' attack on Tanzanian trans woman and activist Mauzinde - found abandoned in a forest, beaten, with her ears cut; the UN office said she had been 'tortured & sexually assaulted by 12 men' and called for bold action against discrimination.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Tanzania's criminalisation of same-sex activity (life imprisonment possible).
NOTE: The OONI report on internet censorship in Tanzania (2024) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

Amnesty International report (Jan 2024) 'We Are Facing Extinction': escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponization of law and their human-rights implications in select African countries - country profiles including Tanzania, Uganda, Kenya, Ghana and others.

Rainer Ebert interview (Sept 2020): 'The LGBT community in Tanzania' - three Tanzanian activists (a lesbian woman, a trans woman, a gay man, all anonymous) describe substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence and denial of basic rights; published with a Swahili version.

Zanzibar Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004 (full text): the criminal code of semiautonomous Zanzibar - includes its sexual-offence provisions criminalising same-sex conduct with penalties up to life imprisonment.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Tanzania: the three most widespread problems were security-force excessive force, gender-based violence including FGM/C, and lack of access to justice; also 'discrimination based on sexual orientation' and societal violence against persons with albinism.

records.name: Uganda
records.summary:
Uganda is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act imposes life imprisonment for same-sex conduct and the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality," and the US State Department explicitly warns that "the law applies to both visitors and residents." Over 1,000 rights violations (arrests, torture, evictions) were documented in nine months. Mobs have gathered outside trans people's homes (one woman described being grabbed and shouted at that she needed to die); police use digital entrapment (obtaining evidence via dating apps); and the government has "spread misinformation and hatred against LGBT people." The law also criminalises the "promotion of homosexuality," meaning any advocacy or support is banned.

There are no laws regulating gender identity — the AHA targets same-sex conduct and promotion, not trans identity per se — but trans people are swept up in the broader anti-LGBT crackdown, mobs, and state violence. The Constitutional Court upheld the AHA in April 2024 (striking down only a few provisions on healthcare access and renting).

Uganda's death penalty is for "aggravated" same-sex (not all same-sex like Iran; not gender expression per se like Saudi), and no trans-specific visitor killing or border-targeting is documented — but the systematic state-led crackdown makes this a environment to avoid entirely.

sources.claim: HRW report 'They're Putting Our Lives at Risk' (May 2025): how Uganda's anti-LGBT climate unleashes abuse - the 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act (death penalty for 'aggravated homosexuality', lengthy sentences for 'promotion') has fuelled arrests, raids on shelters, evictions and public outings; many LGBT people in hiding; a small group of Ugandan mothers began speaking publicly in support of their LGBT children.
Human Rights Watch (Apr 2024): 'Uganda: Court Upholds Anti-Homosexuality Act' — the Constitutional Court keeps the 2023 Act in force, with its life-sentence and 'aggravated' provisions intact.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (June 2024) covers rights violations against Uganda's LGBTQ community escalating, per a pressure group.
The Guardian (Jan 2024): 'If I go out, I'll be a target' - fear stalks Uganda over brutal anti-gay laws; profiles Arianna at a safe house with 20 other transgender people on the outskirts of Kampala.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying US State Department travel advisory for Uganda includes LGBT-specific warnings under the 'Do Not Travel' advisory.
Access Now: Uganda's anti-LGBTQ entrapment laws - analysis of how digital entrapment and surveillance are used against LGBTQ people under the Anti-Homosexuality Act framework.

Amnesty International (Oct 2024): criminalization shrinks online civic space for LGBTQ people in Uganda - the report 'Everybody Here Is Having Two Lives or Phones' documents technology-facilitated gender-based violence (doxing, outing, threats, blackmail, impersonation, hacking, disinformation); the AHA 2023 fostered a climate of impunity, forcing individuals and organisations to alter how they engage online.

AP (Feb 2026): 'Ugandan police arrest two women for allegedly kissing in public' — two women detained in Arua after neighbours reported them; one of the first known arrests under the 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Uganda: the three most important problems included 'violence and discrimination against marginalized groups (women...; children...; persons with disabilities; and the lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender community)' - the era of the Anti-Homosexuality Bill debates.

records.name: Ukraine
records.summary:
Ukraine is workable for trans visitors, with the caveat that this scores trans-specific risk, not the obvious general risks of an active war zone. Ukraine criminalises nothing about being trans; legal gender recognition exists (medicalised — a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation under the 2016 protocol), and a resilient civil society (Gender Stream, Insight) operates openly. Kyiv hosted a three-day Trans Forum in June 2026 even during the war.

Trans-specific frictions exist but mostly affect residents, not visitors: trans women with male passports cannot leave the country under martial law (conscription), and wartime document checks can out people. A foreign visitor's passport is not subject to mobilisation rules, so border crossing is governed by standard wartime entry rules. There is no SOGI-specific hate-crime law, societal attitudes lag EU averages, and the healthcare system is war-disrupted (hormone shortages, diagnostic corruption reported).

Ukraine scores far above Russia (0.12) and Belarus (0.13) — no criminalisation, no state persecution, functioning NGOs — and below Serbia (0.64) and Moldova (0.65), reflecting wartime institutional strain and weaker legal protections rather than active hostility.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch essay (May 2024): 'When Laws Fail to Protect Trans People, Harmful Medicalized Norms Creep In' — examines Ukraine's LGR regime requiring a 'transsexualism' diagnosis and humiliating military-medical-commission confirmation, worsened by wartime displacement.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying France24 piece (June 2022) covers Ukraine's trans community caught in the crosshairs of war.

ZMINA (July 2026): 'Trans women now find it more difficult to obtain a diagnosis' - stereotypes, corruption and other challenges facing transgender people during wartime; interviews from Trans Forum 2026 in Kyiv covering corruption in healthcare, hormone-medication shortages, mobilisation-related problems, risks of the new draft Civil Code, the legal gender-change process, and the transition to ICD-11.

Gender Stream (Ukrainian NGO): consultations and support - advises and accompanies LGBTQI+ people and families during evacuation from combat regions to western Ukraine and the EU; helps with processing/reissuing documents for trans people and legal border crossing; monitors human-rights observance during document processing and travel abroad under martial-law restrictions.

European Parliament written question E-002018/2022 (Jun 2022): on the situation of transgender people in Ukraine amid the Russian invasion, in the context of Parliament's resolution on war's impact on women.

Amnesty International (May 2013): 'Ukraine: Discrimination and violent attacks in pervasive climate of homophobia' - report 'Nothing to be proud of' exposes endemic discrimination; people beaten and one murdered; most crimes uninvestigated; the possibility of attack used as an excuse to deprive LGBTI people of assembly rights; lawmakers urged to reject 'propaganda' bills.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Aug 2016): 'Good news from Malaysia, Namibia, Ukraine' - advances for trans people in Ukraine (alongside Malaysia's ID-card ruling and Namibia's ombudsman comments) per ILGA's LGBulleTIn round-up.
HRW (June 2012): 'Ukraine: Investigate Brutal Attack on Gay Activist' - documents the violent attack on an LGBT activist and calls for investigation amid the 'propaganda' bill debates.
